items.title: Synchron pauses enrollment in trials of its second-generation, fully wireless Stentrode BCI over a lead performance issue and restructures toward San Diego
items.summary: Synchron said it voluntarily paused enrollment in its multisite US trial (with sister sites in Australia and Canada) of the second-generation, fully wireless Stentrode after finding a performance issue with the lead that carries signals from the Stentrode to the implanted electronics; it says no device safety issue was found, the pause was not FDA-directed, and it will upgrade the whole system before resuming. WIRED also reported job cuts and a scaled-back New York footprint as Synchron builds a San Diego team for an upgraded lead and a new device.

details.hub_relevance: A lead failure stalling a leading implanted-BCI program shows that cabling and interconnect reliability, not just electrodes, gate chronic neural-interface timelines, which is relevant to the Hub's engineering reviews of implant and wearable designs.
details.review_notes: First reported by WIRED 11-12 with Synchron statement; corroborated by MassDevice 11-12 and Inside BCI 11-13. Separate from the FOCUS-CAN registry termination (Sep) rejected in earlier runs.

items.title: Open-BEATBox: an open-source autonomous operant chamber for high-throughput data acquisition of complex behaviour
items.summary: Continuous, self-paced home-cage operant testing of complex cognition in mice without daily sessions or food/water restriction (stated aim). The authors built their own open-source, modular platform for this. They state the limits of conventional operant testing: short daily sessions, frequent experimenter intervention, food or water restriction, and disrupted natural activity patterns. They do not state any hardware gap that an outside product would fill. The collaboration angle is inferred from overlap with Hub-led home-cage devices.

people.name: Eric Burguière
people.institution: Paris Brain Institute (ICM) and CNRS - Lyon Neuroscience Research Centre (CRNL), France

people.name: Marine Euvrard
people.institution: Paris Brain Institute (ICM) and CNRS - Lyon Neuroscience Research Centre (CRNL), France

details.facts: Stated (bioRxiv abstract and metadata only; v1 posted 2026-11-10, CC BY-NC 4.0; full text not yet available as JATS/HTML): Open-BEATBox (Open Platform for Experimental Neuroscience Behavioural and Autonomous Box) is an open-source, autonomous home-cage platform for continuous self-paced cognitive testing in mice. It is modular and customizable, supports a range of operant paradigms, and is designed to integrate with chronic neural recording and neuromodulation. In a visual reversal-learning task, continuous testing produced about 10x more completed trials than session-based protocols and reduced experimenter workload, with no evidence of major adverse effects on the welfare measures assessed. An uncertainty-based decision-making task was also implemented. Funding: ANR (ANR-16-INSERM-SINREP, ANR-19-ICM-DOPALOOPS, ANR-21-ICM-PREDICTOC, ANR-24-INSERM-EVOMATIC), Fondation de France, FRM. No competing interests declared. 16 authors (ICM Paris, CRNL Lyon). UPDATE 2026-11-12, from the project's public manual (open-beatbox.github.io/docs/manual; CC BY 4.0) and Zenodo deposits dated 2026-11-09 (hardware 10.5281/zenodo.24080047, software 10.5281/zenodo.24080478, documentation 10.5281/zenodo.24080480): the repositories are public on GitHub (Open-BeatBox org) as release 'biorxiv-v1' (2026-11-03). Licences: hardware CERN-OHL-S-2.0, software AGPL-3.0, documentation and build guides CC BY 4.0. Hardware V3 has CAD files and eight KiCad boards, and real boxes have been built. Modules (feeder, nosepoke, screen, lighting, tunnel/IR barrier, main) each have their own microcontroller and talk over a CAN bus. The main module is an RP2040 board with an RTC and microSD that links to a PC over UART. The feeder module delivers food pellets with a stepper motor (A4988 driver) and detects them with an IR photo-interrupter. The PC app (Qt) runs training stages S1-S4, writes CSV files and controls multiple boxes; the module firmware is MicroPython. The manual's 'Status and open points' page lists open items: incomplete Master BOM (marked 0.1-draft), assembly docs without revision dates, and open validation (final cost benchmark, cable lengths, wall colour for tracking, long-term reliability). Its Contributing page invites outside contributions to hardware, code, stages and validation results.
details.inferences: Open-BEATBox sits in the same home-cage, self-paced operant space as FED3 (supported) and the Hub-led FED4 (in development). It also overlaps topically with the Spatial Foraging Platform (programmable home-cage foraging, in development). The project builds its own stepper-driven pellet feeder, so it is a peer or benchmark for FED3/FED4 pellet delivery, not a buyer. The public repos, copyleft licences, explicit contribution invitation and listed open validation items (long-term reliability, cost benchmark) make a technical exchange more plausible. Examples: FED3/FED4 reliability and pellet-detection experience, shared stage/task designs, or a cross-validation of continuous home-cage operant data. These are still inferences: the authors state no need for outside hardware or help beyond the general contribution invitation. No purchasing intent is assumed.
details.product_matches_raw: FED4 (Feeding Experimentation Device 4); FED3 (Feeding Experimentation Device 3); Spatial Foraging Platform (SFP)
details.recommended_action: Human review: Investigate as an open-source home-cage operant peer project for FED4/SFP collaboration or benchmarking. Repository and manual are now public (CERN-OHL-S hardware, AGPL software). If of interest, a Hub engineer could review the feeder module and open points against FED4. Re-check the bioRxiv full text when posted. No outreach from Scout.
details.review_note: Preprint (not peer reviewed). bioRxiv full text still not posted (re-checked 2026-11-12); the 2026-11-12 update draws on the public manual and Zenodo/GitHub metadata only, with no paper full text. Collab raised 65->70 on 2026-11-12 (openness 10->15: public repos with open licences and an explicit contribution invitation). items.title: Circadian modulation of dopamine release shapes reward-evoked signaling in the nucleus accumbens
items.summary: Multi-day home-cage reward and activity measurement synchronized with long-term fiber photometry across circadian time (LD and DD). The lab built this in-house: custom IR-beam lickometers on a water spout and a 5% sucrose spout, a servo-operated sliding door giving 10 min/h sucrose access, and a custom Arduino-based controller (TageLabs) that triggers photometry, runs the door, and logs timestamped licks to CSV; wheel running was recorded with ClockLab (Actimetrics). No hardware gap or limitation is stated; the need is inferred from the custom-built setup.

details.facts: Stated (bioRxiv preprint 10.64898/2026.04.22.720003 v1 full text, CC BY-NC; published as PNAS Nexus 2026-11-07, CC BY-NC, journal full text blocked 403, abstract matches): mice with NAc DA3m sensor; multi-channel fiber photometry (Neurophotometrics FP3002) recorded for days with 10 min on / 20 min off duty cycle; spontaneous DA peaks in early subjective day; reward-evoked DA peaks near the day-to-night transition; reward behavior peaks in early subjective night; two-spout lickometers (IR beam, 50-100 ms valid-contact filter), hourly lick and bout counts; wheel-running free-running period matched the DA rhythm. Funding: NIH R35GM151020 (J.R.J.), Whitehall Foundation, NIH F31DA065512 (J.N.C.). Analysis code public (github.com/jones-lab-tamu/DA_Photometry_and_Reward_Analysis).

items.title: The hidden impact of cage position on behavioral phenotyping and reproducibility
items.summary: Documenting and controlling lifelong in-cage illumination differences by rack position in a neurobehavioral core (stated: uppermost vs lowermost shelves produced 70 vs 20 lx inside cages; cage position altered exploratory/risk-assessment behavior). Illumination was measured with a spot TES 1332 A digital lux meter (stated method).

people.name: Lior Bikovski
people.institution: Tel Aviv University (Myers Neuro-Behavioral Core Facility / Gray Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences), Tel-Aviv, Israel

people.name: Chaim G. Pick
people.institution: Tel Aviv University (Myers Neuro-Behavioral Core Facility / Gray Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences), Tel-Aviv, Israel

details.facts: Stated (full text, Scientific Reports, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0): male/female ICR mice housed from birth to adulthood on uppermost vs lowermost shelves of an IVC rack at Myers Neuro-Behavioral Core Facility (Tel Aviv University); in-cage light-phase illumination 70 lx (upper) vs 20 lx (lower) by TES 1332 A lux meter; lower-shelf mice left the light-dark box dark compartment faster (survived correction) and showed less EPM risk-assessment; locomotor activity, spatial memory, nociception, and optic-nerve diameter unchanged. Authors conclude cage position is a hidden confounder removable by counterbalancing. Corresponding datasets available from corresponding author on request.
details.inferences: Continuous in-cage light (and activity) logging with Hub Wheel with Hublink or Body Event Analysis Module 3 (BEAM3) could replace or supplement spot lux-meter checks and document developmental light exposure across many cages in a core facility. Equivalence of Hub light sensors to the TES 1332 A readings is untested. No purchasing intent or tooling gap is stated; the study is complete.

items.summary: Continuous home-cage circadian activity monitoring of mice undergoing daily operant/touchscreen testing, with control of chamber and home-cage lighting (stated method); authors state individual activity records were not available for pair-housed females because overhead PIR sensors give a cage-level aggregate (stated limitation).

details.facts: Stated (full text, bioRxiv preprint, CC BY-NC 4.0): Bussey-Saksida touchscreen chambers (Campden/Lafayette ABET II, Whisker); home-cage locomotor activity by overhead passive-infrared sensors with ClockLab (Actimetrics); standard screen light (~21 lux) caused ~3.5 h phase delay after 7 days of early-dark testing; 10 lighting conditions tested; recommendations include treating the chamber as a light source, brighter home-cage lighting, removing short-wavelength light, periodic DD probes. items.title: Hub-assembled Tumbly kit for time-restricted feeding, launched off the new preprint
items.summary: The Tumbly preprint (bioRxiv, posted Oct 24, 2026; Barrett, ..., Gaidica, ..., Musiek, Kravitz) reports no device failures over >1000 h in two labs, battery power, and a swappable faceplate for different home cages. TRF is common in metabolism, circadian, aging, and neurodegeneration work. Commercial timed feeders exist but are priced or wired for facilities: TageLabs AutoFeeder lists $384 each (1-9 units); FeedTime, Phenome, and Intellibio feeders are lid- or cabinet-based with no public price. Many labs can't build from design files, and the Hub already sells assembled open-source devices from the same Kravitz lineage (Sipper Hub). A Hublink version (Hublink-Node-Tumbly board) could add wireless logging. Demand and IP/licensing terms (GPL design, OTM) are not verified.

items.title: Wireless fleet data retrieval for the FED3 installed base
items.summary: FED3 logs to an on-board microSD card, so labs running many cages collect data by hand. The Hub's own Nov 2024 post estimates 100+ labs and 3,000+ FED3 devices. On FEDforum, users have built one-off Wi-Fi workarounds, and FED's developer called multi-device wireless harvesting 'not trivial'. Users also report university IT network restrictions that block ESP32 Wi-Fi devices. Hublink's BLE gateway sidesteps campus Wi-Fi, already has a FED3 integration path (ESP32-S3 Feather + SD backpack + multi-architecture FED3 library), and FED4 v1.7 lists optional Hublink BLE sync. Need is documented; willingness to pay for a retrofit or subscription is untested.

details.hub_asset: Hublink + FED3 (supported) + FED4 (in development, optional Hublink BLE sync)
details.potential_value: Strategic: a large installed base reachable through existing Hub software; possible retrofit kit or Hublink subscription revenue (amount unknown)
details.recommended_action: Count Hublink-connected FED3 users today, then decide whether to package a FED3-Hublink retrofit kit as a store SKU or wait for FED4 release; no external outreach until decided

items.title: Cage-scale programmable spatial foraging compatible with chronic neural recording
items.summary: Open naturalistic-foraging platforms are either room-scale or head-fixed. SWC's Aeon habitat is about 2.7 x 2.4 m with wheel-based foraging patches. Dynamic-foraging tasks such as Allen's are rig-based. FED3 offers single-location operant feeding in the home cage. No widely adopted tool appears to turn a standard home-cage floor into a distributed, programmable reward and cue field that works with chronic recordings, which is SFP's design. This is a hypothesis from a desk scan, not a validated gap: no user survey or demand data yet, and SFP is alpha stage and not for sale.
